transcripts.slide_title: Is Global Warming Fake if it Snows?
transcripts.transcript: If you walk outside and it's snowing, you might hear someone joke, 'So much for global warming!' But this represents a fundamental misunderstanding of how the Earth works. A single snowstorm in one city doesn't invalidate a global trend. To put things in perspective, despite any local cold snaps, proxy data shows that 2023 was the hottest year on Earth in over one hundred and twenty-five thousand years.

Let's formally separate these two ideas. Weather describes the short-term, local atmospheric conditions—what you see when you look out the window right now, like rain or sunshine. Climate, on the other hand, is the long-term statistical average of those conditions over a specific region. While weather changes minute by minute, climate is typically measured in trends spanning thirty years or more.

To lock this in your memory, let's use a relatable analogy. Think of weather as your current mood. You might wake up grumpy one day and be ecstatic the next; it changes rapidly. Climate is your overall personality. Even if a generally optimistic person has one bad day, their baseline personality remains positive. Similarly, a cold day doesn't mean the climate isn't warming.

A common trap—and our non-example for today—is using a single cold temperature reading to claim the climate is cooling. In science, climate relies on statistical averages, represented mathematically as the mean of many years of data. When the baseline average shifts upwards, you can still have individual days that are below average. The existence of an outlier does not erase the mathematical reality of a shifting, warming baseline.

To truly understand global warming, we have to recognize the fundamental difference between weather and climate. People often confuse the two, mistakenly assuming that a remarkably cold day means the Earth isn't warming. In this section, we will look at clear, real-world examples to help you instantly identify whether you are looking at a short-term weather event or a long-term climate pattern.

Let's start by looking at weather. A sudden thunderstorm rolling in on a Tuesday afternoon, or a freezing weekend in Texas, are perfect examples of weather. These are short-term, highly localized conditions that can change rapidly from one day to the next. They tell us exactly what is happening outside right now, but they do not define the baseline normal of a region.

In contrast, climate is the statistical average of weather over a long period, usually at least $30$ years. For instance, the Sahara Desert receives less than $3$ inches of rain per year on average over the last century. That consistency over decades is what defines a climate. Even if it happens to rain one afternoon in the Sahara—which is weather—its overall climate remains profoundly dry.

Let's compare these side-by-side to solidify this mental model. A freezing weekend in Texas is a localized weather anomaly; it is an isolated event, not a trend. A century of drought in the Sahara is a climate reality based on statistical data. A crucial non-example to remember is that a single unusually hot summer day does not, by itself, prove global warming. We must always look at decades of data to make accurate claims about the climate.

If it snowed today, does that mean global warming is a hoax? This is what we call the Cold Day Fallacy. It happens when people confuse what is happening right now outside their window with long-term global trends. A local cold snap tells us nothing about the Earth's overall rising temperature.

To break this down, we must clearly define weather versus climate. Weather is short-term and local, like the rain or snow you see on a given Tuesday. Climate, however, is the long-term statistical average of these conditions over decades. Think of it this way: weather is your current mood, while climate is your overall personality. You might have a sad day, but generally still be a happy person.

Let's look at a strict non-example of climate: a severe winter snowstorm. A snowstorm is simply weather. You cannot use one isolated cold day to invalidate a decades-long global warming trend. In science, a single local data point never overrides the statistical average of thousands of data points collected worldwide.

When we zoom out and look at the actual climate, the baseline reality becomes undeniable. Despite occasional cold snaps or snowstorms, the overarching global trend is rapidly warming. In fact, historical proxy data reveals that 2023 was the hottest year in over 125,000 years. We must always rely on these long-term statistical trends, rather than our daily weather, to truly understand global climate change.

When we look at the world around us, we constantly experience meteorological events, from sudden rainstorms to long-term droughts. The challenge is correctly classifying these observations so we can make sense of what is actually happening to our planet. To do this accurately, we must focus on the time scale of the event rather than just its intensity. Let's learn how to apply the 'timeline test' to categorize these events.

The fundamental rule for categorizing meteorological data is the timeline test. If an observation spans a period of hours, days, or even a few weeks, you are looking at weather. However, in atmospheric science, the standard period to determine a climate baseline is 30 years of data. If your observation involves analyzing a statistical trend over decades, you are evaluating climate.

Let's apply this concept to a specific real-world example. Consider the statement: 'The Pacific Northwest has experienced progressively wetter winters over the past 30 years.' Ask yourself what the timeline is here. Because this statement tracks a statistical trend over a long, multi-decade period, it is firmly an observation of climate. We are not looking at a single stormy winter, but a sustained shift in the region's long-term baseline.

It is crucial to build a strong mental model of what climate is NOT. For instance, experiencing a massive, record-breaking blizzard today does not mean global warming has stopped. That blizzard is a single weather event, highly localized in time. While climate change might make extreme weather events more frequent or severe, the isolated event itself is just weather. Always zoom out and look for the statistical trend to accurately assess the climate.
